questions.accessiblePrompt: A company says its new process turns 300 grams of reactants into 206 grams of medicine, and makes the other 94 grams simply disappear, so there is no waste. What is the best response to this claim?

choices.text: It could be right if the process runs in a sealed container.
choices.rationale: A sealed container would keep the 94 g inside, where a balance would still count it.

choices.text: It could be right because the extra atoms turn into energy.
choices.rationale: Ordinary chemical reactions do not turn measurable amounts of mass into energy.

choices.text: It can't be right: the 94 g of atoms must end up somewhere.
choices.rationale: Correct: atoms are conserved, so 94 g of other products must exist; they are waste unless put to use.

choices.text: It can't be right: the medicine alone should have a mass of 300 g.
choices.rationale: Only all the products together must total 300 g; the medicine is one product, so 206 g of it is possible. The real problem is the claim that 94 g vanished.

questions.explanation: Every gram of reactants has to show up in the products. If only 206 g is medicine, the other 94 g is in other substances. Those are waste unless the company finds a use for them, which is exactly what green chemistry tries to do.
questions.misconception: Unwanted matter can vanish if a process is designed cleverly enough.
questions.hint: Use conservation of mass: what must the products add up to?

evidence.supports: Matter cannot be created or destroyed; the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products.
Because matter is conserved, chemical manufacturing produces waste unless processes are redesigned.

evidence.title: Chemistry 2e, 21.1 Nuclear Structure and Stability
evidence.supports: Mass changes during ordinary chemical reactions are virtually undetectable.

questions.prompt: Three test designs make the same product. Using the table, which design puts the largest share of its reactants' mass into the wanted product?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Three test designs make the same product. Design A uses 400 grams of reactants and makes 240 grams of product and 160 grams of waste. Design B uses 300 grams of reactants and makes 210 grams of product and 90 grams of waste. Design C uses 150 grams of reactants and makes 90 grams of product and 60 grams of waste. Which design puts the largest share of its reactants' mass into the wanted product?

choices.text: Design A
choices.rationale: A makes the most grams, but 240 ÷ 400 is only 60% of its reactant mass.

choices.text: Design B
choices.rationale: Correct: 210 ÷ 300 = 70%, the largest share of the three.

choices.text: Design C
choices.rationale: C has the least waste in grams only because it is the smallest run; 90 ÷ 150 is 60%.

choices.text: Can't tell without knowing which runs fastest
choices.rationale: Speed is not needed; the share comes straight from the masses.

diagram.caption: Test results for three designs
diagram.alt: Table. Design A: 400 g reactants, 240 g wanted product, 160 g waste. Design B: 300 g reactants, 210 g wanted product, 90 g waste. Design C: 150 g reactants, 90 g wanted product, 60 g waste.

questions.explanation: Compare shares, not raw amounts: A is 240/400 = 60%, B is 210/300 = 70%, and C is 90/150 = 60%. B sends the largest share of its reactant mass into the product. Comparing designs with the same yardstick is how the ibuprofen engineers judged their options.
questions.misconception: The design that makes the most product, or the least waste in grams, must be the most efficient.
questions.hint: The designs use different amounts of reactants. How could you compare them fairly?

questions.prompt: Look at how the atoms regroup in CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CO₂ + H₂O + CaCl₂. Which description fits best?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Look at how the atoms regroup in this reaction: C a C O 3, calcium carbonate, plus 2 H C l, hydrogen chloride, yields C O 2, carbon dioxide, plus H 2 O, water, plus C a C l 2, calcium chloride. Which description fits best?

choices.text: Joining together, since two substances react.
choices.rationale: Joining together ends with one product, but this reaction ends with three.

choices.text: Breaking apart, since three substances form.
choices.rationale: Breaking apart starts from one substance, but this reaction starts with two.

choices.text: A swap plus a join, since calcium and chlorine end up together.
choices.rationale: Calcium pairing with chlorine is the swap itself; a swap keeps two substances, and a join would leave fewer, not three.

choices.text: A swap plus a break-up, since two substances become three.
choices.rationale: Correct: calcium and hydrogen trade partners (a swap), and the hydrogen-and-carbonate group then splits into CO₂ and H₂O (a break-up).

diagram.caption: Calcium carbonate reacting with hydrogen chloride
diagram.alt: Equation: C a C O 3, calcium carbonate, plus 2 H C l, hydrogen chloride, yields C O 2, carbon dioxide, plus H 2 O, water, plus C a C l 2, calcium chloride. Two substances react and three substances form.

questions.conditions: Use this lesson's three patterns: breaking apart (one substance becomes two or more), joining together (two or more become one), and swapping partners (two substances trade partners to make two new ones).
questions.limitations: The patterns describe where the atoms end up, not every step of the real reaction. Calcium carbonate and calcium chloride are ionic extended structures counted in formula units.
questions.explanation: Count the substances: two go in and three come out. A swap alone keeps two, joining makes one, and breaking apart starts from one, so no single pattern fits. Calcium and hydrogen trade partners, and the hydrogen-and-carbonate group, a short-lived substance chemists call carbonic acid, then breaks apart into water and carbon dioxide.
questions.misconception: Every reaction fits exactly one regrouping pattern, judged from one side of the arrow.
questions.hint: Count the substances on each side of the arrow. What does each pattern do to that count?

scope.section: 2. Ways Atoms Regroup in Chemical Reactions

evidence.supports: Besides breaking apart, joining or swapping, atoms can regroup through a mix of these patterns.

questions.prompt: A team tested three designs for making 100 g of a fabric dye. No design won both tests. Using the table, which plan for the next design do the data support best?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A team tested three designs for making 100 grams of a fabric dye. Design X needs 130 grams of reactants and puts none of its leftover mass to use. Design Y needs 200 grams of reactants and puts 80 percent of its leftover mass to use. Design Z needs 200 grams of reactants and puts none of its leftover mass to use. No design won both tests. Which plan for the next design do the data support best?

choices.text: Copy design X, since it needs the least reactant mass.
choices.rationale: X wins the first test but throws away all 30 g of its leftovers; copying it alone keeps that waste.

choices.text: Copy design Y, since it puts the most leftovers to use.
choices.rationale: Y wins the second test, but it needs 200 g of reactants, leaving 100 g of leftovers to deal with.

choices.text: Combine X's route with Y's way of reusing leftovers.
choices.rationale: Correct: X's route leaves the fewest leftovers and Y's method puts most leftovers to use, so a design with both should waste the least.

choices.text: Combine Y's route with Z's way of handling leftovers.
choices.rationale: This mix keeps the weaker result on both tests: Y's route needs more reactant than X's, and Z reuses nothing.

diagram.caption: Test results for three dye designs (each makes 100 g of dye)
diagram.alt: Table. Each design makes 100 grams of the same dye. Design X: needs 130 grams of reactants and puts 0 percent of its leftover mass to use. Design Y: needs 200 grams of reactants and puts 80 percent of its leftover mass to use. Design Z: needs 200 grams of reactants and puts 0 percent of its leftover mass to use.

questions.conditions: Each design makes 100 g of the same dye. Assume Y's way of reusing leftovers would work on the other designs' leftovers too.
questions.limitations: Hypothetical test data. A combined design is a plan to test next, not a guaranteed result.
questions.explanation: No design wins every test, so look at which feature wins each one. X's route needs the least reactant mass, and Y's method puts the most leftovers to use. Combining them should leave only about 6 g of waste per batch (30 g of leftovers with 80% reused), less than X's 30 g, Y's 20 g or Z's 100 g, though the team would still need to test it.
questions.misconception: The best plan is to copy whichever single design wins one test, or to combine any two designs.
questions.hint: Find which design did best on each test. What feature gave it that result?

evidence.locator: Next Generation Science Standards box (MS-ETS1-3; ETS1.B; ETS1.C)
evidence.supports: When no design performs best on every test, the features that did best on each test can be combined into a new design that beats its predecessors.
Engineers analyzed their data and combined the best characteristics of two solutions to reach a process that better met their criteria.
